A nonempty open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ is **star-shaped with respect to** $a\in U$ when

$$a+t(x-a)\in U\qquad\text{for every }x\in U\text{ and }0\le t\le1.$$

The point $a$ is a **star centre**. Every convex open set of [[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]] is star-shaped with respect to each of its points. The nonemptiness and the chosen centre are part of the definition.

Let $F:M\to N$ be smooth, and let $\omega\in\Omega^k(N)$. The **pullback**
$F^*\omega$ is the pullback of $\omega$ viewed as an alternating covariant
$k$-tensor field:

$$ (F^*\omega)_p(v_1,\ldots,v_k)=\omega_{F(p)}(dF_pv_1,\ldots,dF_pv_k). $$
For every smooth map $F:M\to N$ and every form $\omega$ on $N$, $$d(F^*\omega)=F^*(d\omega).$$

Let $a<b$ and $c<d$. Suppose $g,h:[a,b]\times[c,d]\to\mathbb R$ are continuous and, for every fixed $t\in[c,d]$, the function $x\mapsto g(x,t)$ is differentiable on $(a,b)$ with derivative $h(x,t)$. Define

$$G(x):=\int_c^d g(x,t)\,dt.$$

Then $G$ is differentiable on $[a,b]$ as a function on that interval and

$$G'(x)=\int_c^d h(x,t)\,dt\qquad(x\in[a,b]).$$

At $a$ and $b$ the derivative is relative and one-sided. The derivative hypothesis is imposed only for interior parameter values; continuity of $h$ supplies its endpoint values.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: Define $F:(0,1)\times U\to U$ by $F(t,x)=a+t(x-a)$. By [F1] this map has image in $U$, and both its domain and target are boundaryless smooth manifolds, so [F3] applies to this restriction. In product coordinates decompose $F^*\alpha=\gamma_t+dt\wedge\eta_t$, where $\gamma_t$ is a $k$-form and $\eta_t$ a $(k-1)$-form on $U$. The same affine formula, viewed first as a map $\bar F:\mathbb R\times U\to\mathbb R^n$, has image in $U$ on a neighborhood of every $(t_0,x_0)$ with $0\le t_0\le1$, because $\bar F(t_0,x_0)\in U$ and $U$ is open. Thus the coefficient formulas for $\gamma_t$ and $\eta_t$ extend smoothly to $t=0,1$ locally in $(t,x)$.

The integrand defining $K\alpha$ is alternating and multilinear in $v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}$, so its integral is a $(k-1)$-covariant alternating tensor at each $x$. Its coefficient functions are smooth in $(x,t)$. Restricting $x$ to a compact coordinate rectangle inside $U$ and using [F4] on each coordinate derivative shows that parameter derivatives pass through the $t$-integral; iteration gives smooth coefficients, hence a smooth $(k-1)$-form $K\alpha$.

Since $d\alpha=0$, [F3] gives $d(F^*\alpha)=0$ on $(0,1)\times U$. In product coordinates $d=d_U+dt\wedge\partial_t$, so the coefficient of $dt$ is $\partial_t\gamma_t-d_U\eta_t=0$ for $0<t<1$. By the local smooth extension in step 1.1, this coefficient identity extends by continuity to $t=0,1$. The pullback formula [F2] gives $(\eta_t)_x(v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1}) =t^{k-1}\alpha_{a+t(x-a)}(x-a,v_1,\ldots,v_{k-1})$ for interior $t$, and then also at the endpoints by continuity.

Thus $K\alpha=\int_0^1\eta_t\,dt$. By step 2.1 and [F4], $d_U\int_0^1\eta_t\,dt=\int_0^1d_U\eta_t\,dt$. Apply [F5] to the coefficient functions of $\gamma_t$ and use step 2.2: $\gamma_1-\gamma_0=\int_0^1\partial_t\gamma_t\,dt =d_U\int_0^1\eta_t\,dt$. Here $\gamma_1=\alpha$ because $F(1,x)=x$, while $\gamma_0=0$ because $F(0,x)=a$ is constant and $k\ge1$. Hence $d(K\alpha)=\alpha$.

For a smooth manifold $M$, possibly with boundary, let
$$C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\mathbb R^{(S_k^\infty(M))}\quad(k\ge0),\qquad C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=0\quad(k<0),$$
using [[def-smooth-singular-simplex]]. It is the subspace of [[def-real-singular-chain-complex]] spanned by the smooth simplices, with the same signed face differential.

This is a subcomplex: an affine face map $\delta_i:A^{k-1}\to A^k$ has the open inverse image $\delta_i^{-1}(O)$ containing $\Delta^{k-1}$. Composing $\bar\sigma$ with this affine map on that inverse image extends $\sigma\delta_i$ smoothly into $M$. Thus every face is smooth, and the already proved signed cancellation gives $\partial^2=0$ on this subspace.

Define the **smooth singular cochain complex** by
$$C_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathbb R}(C_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R),\mathbb R),\qquad \delta\varphi=\varphi\partial.$$
As for [[def-real-singular-cochain-complex]], these are arbitrary real functions on the supplied smooth-simplex basis, evaluated by finite sums. Precomposition gives $\delta^2\varphi=\varphi\partial^2=0$. Define $H_k^\infty(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\partial_k/\operatorname{im}\partial_{k+1}$ and $H_\infty^k(M;\mathbb R)=\ker\delta^k/\operatorname{im}\delta^{k-1}$; both quotients are licensed by square-zero.

Negative groups vanish and the degree-zero boundary is zero. On a point all simplices are smooth, so the complexes are the ordinary unnormalized point complexes; no constant simplices are discarded. For the empty manifold all groups are zero. The specified subspaces and duals require no choice of extensions or bases.

Let $\sigma:\Delta^k\to M$ be a smooth singular simplex and let $\omega$ be a smooth $k$-form on an open neighbourhood of its image in $M$. For $k\ge1$ put
$$T_k=\{x\in\mathbb R^k:x_j\ge0,\ \sum_jx_j\le1\},\qquad a(x)=v_0+\sum_{j=1}^kx_j(v_j-v_0).$$
Take a smooth extension $\bar\sigma$ near $\Delta^k$, restrict its domain so that $\omega$ is defined on its image, and write $a^*\bar\sigma^*\omega=f(x)\,dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_k$. Define
$$\int_\sigma\omega:=\int_{T_k}f(x)\,dx.$$
The right side is the Jordan-set Riemann integral. In degree zero define $\int_\sigma\omega=\omega(\sigma(v_0))$. This fixes the positive point convention. Reversing the domain orientation negates the integral. Independence of other positive affine coordinates is the forward justification [[lem-simplex-integrals-are-independent-of-affine-coordinate-identification]].

Let $E\subseteq\mathbb R^m$ be bounded in the metric sense of
[[def-metric-bounded-diameter]] and Jordan measurable, and let
$f:E\to\mathbb R$ be bounded. Choose a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\supseteq E$, whose existence follows from
[[def-jordan-inner-and-outer-content]], and define the zero extension
$$\widetilde f_Q(x):=\begin{cases}f(x),&x\in E,\\0,&x\in Q\setminus E.\end{cases}$$
The function $f$ is **Riemann integrable over $E$** when $\widetilde f_Q$ is integrable over $Q$, and then
$$\int_Ef:=\int_Q\widetilde f_Q.$$
Independence of the bounding rectangle, for both integrability and value, is proved in [[lem-jordan-set-integral-well-defined]] and recorded as the definition's forward justification. For $f=1$, the zero extension is $1_E$, so [[thm-jordan-content-and-indicator-integrability]] gives $\int_E1=\operatorname{cont}(E)$.

For a bounded function $f:Q\to\mathbb R$ on a nondegenerate rectangle
$Q\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, define
$$\underline{\int_Q}f:=\sup_P L(f,P),\qquad \overline{\int_Q}f:=\inf_P U(f,P),$$
over all grid partitions $P$ of $Q$. The grid family is nonempty, since the endpoints in each coordinate give a one-cell grid. Every lower sum is at most every upper sum by a common refinement and [[lem-multidimensional-refinement-inequalities]], so the two sets of sums are nonempty and bounded and the extrema exist ([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[thm-infimum-property]], [[def-infimum]], [[lem-sup-unique]]).

The function is **Riemann integrable over $Q$** when the two values agree.
Their unique common real is $\int_Q f$. No integral is defined here for a
degenerate rectangle, because the grid definition requires every coordinate
interval to have distinct endpoints. This is the multidimensional Darboux
definition; its agreement with the published one-dimensional definition is
proved separately.

Fix a natural number $m\ge1$. For $a,b\in\mathbb R^m$ with $a_j\le b_j$ for $j<m$, define
$$[a,b]:=\{x\in\mathbb R^m:a_j\le x_j\le b_j\ (j<m)\},\qquad \operatorname{vol}[a,b]:=\prod_{j<m}(b_j-a_j).$$
The product is the recursively defined finite product of [[def-finite-sum]]. The rectangle is **nondegenerate** when every $a_j<b_j$, and it is a **cube** when all side lengths are equal.

Every factor is nonnegative, so volume is nonnegative. For a coordinate index $r<m$, cutting at $c\in[a_r,b_r]$ gives two rectangles whose volumes add to the original, by distributivity in that factor and [[lem-finite-sum-laws]]. Under the standard identification $\mathbb R^1\cong\mathbb R$ ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]], [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]), this is the interval $[a_0,b_0]$ and its length.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
($\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   (The metric topology: a set is open when every one of its points has a ball around it inside the set; closed means open complement) and bounded
   (Bounded subset, diameter, distance from a point to a set, and distance between two sets in a metric space).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   (The absolute value makes $\mathbb{R}$ a metric space: $d(x,y) = |x-y|$ is a metric, its open balls are the intervals $(x-r, x+r)$, and it is unbounded), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
(A complete, totally bounded metric space is compact, proved from countable choice used exactly once) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from $\mathbb{R}^n$ as the set of functions $n \to \mathbb{R}$, and $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ are metrics on it, which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X,d_X)$ be a compact metric space (Open cover, subcover, compact metric space, and compact subset of a metric space), let
$(Y,d_Y)$ be any metric space (Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric) and let $f : X \to Y$ be
continuous (Continuity of a map between metric spaces, at a point and globally, in the $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ form). Then $f$ is uniformly continuous
(Uniform continuity of a map of metric spaces: one $\delta$ serving every point).

No choice principle is used: the cover built below is cut out by a property, and
the Lebesgue number lemma it is fed to is itself choice free
(Every open cover of a compact metric space has a Lebesgue number: a $\delta > 0$ such that every nonempty subset of diameter less than $\delta$ lies inside a single member of the cover).

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

derivations.claim: First consider integration on one simplex, using the zero extension in [F3] to a bounded nondegenerate rectangle $Q$. The Darboux definitions [F4] give linearity: for integrable $u,w$, choose grid partitions whose upper-minus lower sums for each are arbitrarily small, take a common refinement, and use $\inf(u+w)\ge\inf u+\inf w$ and $\sup(u+w)\le\sup u+\sup w$ on each cell. The upper-minus-lower gap for $u+w$ is therefore bounded by the sum of the chosen gaps, so $u+w$ is integrable. Its lower and upper integrals are squeezed between the sums of the lower integrals of $u,w$ and the sums of their upper integrals; letting the gaps tend to zero gives $\int_Q(u+w)=\int_Qu+\int_Qw$. For a scalar $c>0$, upper and lower sums scale by $c$; for $c<0$ they exchange after scaling, giving $\int_Q(cu)=c\int_Qu$, and $c=0$ gives zero. Also, if $|u|\le\varepsilon$ on $Q$, each lower sum is at least $-\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ and each upper sum at most $\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$, since cell volumes add to $\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ by [F5]. Thus $|\int_\sigma u|\le\varepsilon\operatorname{vol}(Q)$ for an integrable function on the simplex bounded by $\varepsilon$.

Fix a parameter chart and a point $p$. For one simplex $\sigma$ write $\sigma^*\alpha_p=f(p,z)\,dz_1\wedge dz_2\wedge dz_3$ on $T_3$. Choose a closed parameter rectangle $R$ around $p$ inside the chart. The displayed inequalities defining $T_3$ make it closed and bounded, hence compact by [F6]; [F2] identifies it as the integration domain. The product $R\times T_3$ is a closed bounded Euclidean set, hence compact by [F6], so $\partial_a f$ is uniformly continuous there by [F7]. For a small nonzero increment $h$ in coordinate $p^a$, [F8] gives $$\frac{f(p+he_a,z)-f(p,z)}{h}-\partial_af(p,z) =\frac1h\int_0^h\bigl(\partial_af(p+se_a,z)-\partial_af(p,z)\bigr)\,ds.$$ Uniform continuity makes the right side tend uniformly to zero on $T_3$ as $h\to0$. By step 1.1, the integral of this error tends to zero. Linearity therefore gives $$\partial_a\int_\sigma f(p,z)\,dz=\int_\sigma\partial_af(p,z)\,dz.$$ Applying the same argument to every parameter derivative of $f$ proves that all parameter partial derivatives of the simplex integral exist and are integrals of the corresponding derivatives. They are continuous: on a compact parameter rectangle, uniform continuity of each next derivative and step 1.1 bound the change in its integral by the uniform coefficient change times $\operatorname{vol}(Q)$. Hence this simplex integral is smooth.

By [F1], $\Sigma$ is a finite linear combination of such simplices. Linearity from step 1.1 makes $I$ the corresponding finite linear combination of their smooth integrals and gives the asserted derivative formula for every parameter coordinate. Linearity in the tangent vector then gives the formula for every $v\in T_pP$.

Let $M$ be an oriented smooth four-manifold and let $\phi$ be a field
configuration in a specified smooth field bundle. A **local Lagrangian
four-form** $\mathcal L(\phi)$ is a smooth four-form whose coordinate
coefficients depend smoothly on the field components and finitely many
spacetime derivatives at each point. A **chosen first-variation
decomposition** consists of a linear Euler functional $E_\phi[\eta]$ with
values in four-forms and a three-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, each linear in the
field variation $\eta$ and its derivatives, such that every smooth
one-parameter field family satisfies

$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi).$$

The choice is part of the data; it is not asserted to be unique. In a
parameter family, $\delta_iE_\phi$ means the derivative of the coefficients
of $E_\phi$ with its variation input held fixed. Thus the total derivative of
$E_{\phi(p)}[\eta(p)]$ is
$(\delta_iE_\phi)[\eta]+E_\phi[\delta_i\eta]$. For a smooth
finite-dimensional field family with parameter exterior derivative $d_P$,
the one-form $\Theta$ on parameter space with values in spacetime three-forms
is $\Theta_p(v)=\theta(\phi_p;\delta_v\phi_p)$. Define the **covariant
presymplectic current** by $\omega:=-d_P\Theta$. For commuting parameter
coordinates $s_1,s_2$ this is

$$\omega(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi) =\delta_2\theta(\phi;\delta_1\phi) -\delta_1\theta(\phi;\delta_2\phi).$$

For a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define the
integrated two-form by
$\Omega_\Sigma(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi)=\int_\Sigma\omega$.

Let $M$ be a smooth four-manifold and let $\pi:E\to M$ be a smooth fibre
bundle. A **field configuration** is a smooth section $\phi:M\to E$, so
$\pi\circ\phi=\operatorname{id}_M$. For a finite-dimensional smooth manifold
$P$, a **smooth field family** is a smooth map
$\Phi:P\times M\to E$ with $\pi(\Phi(p,x))=x$ for all $(p,x)$; it gives
configurations $\phi_p(x)=\Phi(p,x)$. For $u\in T_pP$, the **variation**
$\delta_u\phi_p$ at $x$ is the tangent vector
$d(r\mapsto\Phi(c(r),x))|_{r=0}$, where $c(0)=p$ and $c'(0)=u$. In a local
fibre chart this is the ordinary derivative of the field components with
respect to the parameter. For commuting parameter coordinates $s_1,s_2$,
$\delta_i\phi=\partial_{s_i}\phi$ and
$\delta_1\delta_2\phi=\delta_2\delta_1\phi$.

derivations.claim: Differentiate [A1] in direction $\delta_1$ with input $\delta_2\phi$ held fixed, and in direction $\delta_2$ with input $\delta_1\phi$ held fixed. The total derivatives of the Euler terms are respectively $(\delta_1E_\phi)[\delta_2\phi]+E_\phi[\delta_1\delta_2\phi]$ and $(\delta_2E_\phi)[\delta_1\phi]+E_\phi[\delta_2\delta_1\phi]$ by the definition of $\delta_iE_\phi$ in [A1]. Subtract the second differentiated identity from the first. The second-variation terms cancel by [A2], and the left-hand sides cancel by commutation of mixed derivatives. Since $\omega(\delta_1,\delta_2)=\delta_2\theta(\delta_1)-\delta_1\theta(\delta_2)$, the remaining identity is $$0=(\delta_1E_\phi)[\delta_2\phi]-(\delta_2E_\phi)[\delta_1\phi] -d_M\omega(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi).$$
Rearranging step 1.1 gives $d_M\omega=(\delta_1E_\phi)[\delta_2\phi]-(\delta_2E_\phi)[\delta_1\phi]$, with the stated sign fixed by the Iyer–Wald ordering in [A1].

values in four-forms and a three-form $\theta(\phi;\eta)$, each linear in the
field variation $\eta$ and its derivatives, such that every smooth
one-parameter field family satisfies

$$\delta\mathcal L=E_\phi[\delta\phi]+d_M\theta(\phi;\delta\phi).$$

The choice is part of the data; it is not asserted to be unique. In a
parameter family, $\delta_iE_\phi$ means the derivative of the coefficients
of $E_\phi$ with its variation input held fixed. Thus the total derivative of
$E_{\phi(p)}[\eta(p)]$ is
$(\delta_iE_\phi)[\eta]+E_\phi[\delta_i\eta]$. For a smooth
finite-dimensional field family with parameter exterior derivative $d_P$,
the one-form $\Theta$ on parameter space with values in spacetime three-forms
is $\Theta_p(v)=\theta(\phi_p;\delta_v\phi_p)$. Define the **covariant
presymplectic current** by $\omega:=-d_P\Theta$. For commuting parameter
coordinates $s_1,s_2$ this is

$$\omega(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi) =\delta_2\theta(\phi;\delta_1\phi) -\delta_1\theta(\phi;\delta_2\phi).$$

For a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$, define the
integrated two-form by
$\Omega_\Sigma(\delta_1\phi,\delta_2\phi)=\int_\Sigma\omega$.

Let $\mathcal L$ have a chosen first-variation decomposition with Euler
functional $E_\phi$. If $E_\phi=0$ and both variations satisfy the
linearized equations, so $\delta_iE_\phi=0$, then $d_M\omega=0$. For a finite
oriented smooth singular four-chain $C$ with
$\partial C=\Sigma_2-\Sigma_1+B$, where the $\Sigma_i$ are oriented
three-chains and $B$ is the remaining oriented boundary chain,

$$\Omega_{\Sigma_2}-\Omega_{\Sigma_1}=-\int_B\omega.$$

Thus on-shell closure alone gives independence between cuts only when the
side flux vanishes.

For a fixed smooth two-parameter family of commuting variations, replace the
Lagrangian and its selected potential by

$$\mathcal L'=\mathcal L+d_M\mu,\qquad \theta'(\phi;\delta\phi) =\theta(\phi;\delta\phi)+\delta\mu(\phi;\delta\phi) +d_MY(\phi;\delta\phi),$$

where $\mu$ is a local spacetime three-form and $Y$ is a local spacetime
two-form linear in the variation. Then

$$\omega'-\omega =d_M\bigl(\delta_2Y(\delta_1\phi)-\delta_1Y(\delta_2\phi)\bigr).$$

Consequently, for a finite oriented smooth singular three-chain $\Sigma$,
the integrated form changes by the integral of this two-form over
$\partial\Sigma$.

Let $\mathcal S$ be a specified finite-dimensional smooth solution manifold
with specified admissible variations and boundary conditions, and let
$\Omega$ be a smooth closed two-form on $\mathcal S$, obtained by restricting
an integrated form $\Omega_\Sigma$ from the chosen covariant variation data.
The pair $(\mathcal S,\Omega)$ is **presymplectic** when $\Omega$ is allowed
to be degenerate. At $p\in\mathcal S$, its pointwise null space is
$$\ker\Omega_p:=\{v\in T_p\mathcal S:\Omega_p(v,w)=0 \text{ for every }w\in T_p\mathcal S\}.$$
A **presymplectic reduction** is defined here only when there is a specified
smooth Hausdorff manifold $\mathcal R$ and a surjective submersion
$q:\mathcal S\to\mathcal R$ with connected fibers such that
$$\ker(dq_p)=\ker\Omega_p\qquad(p\in\mathcal S),$$
where $\ker(dq_p)$ consists of tangent vectors mapped to zero by the
differential. This condition makes the quotient fibers exactly the connected
directions annihilated by $\Omega$. The reduction further requires a smooth
closed nondegenerate two-form $\bar\Omega$ on $\mathcal R$ satisfying
$q^*\bar\Omega=\Omega$. For a smooth vector field $X$ and smooth function
$H$ on a specified phase space, the Hamiltonian convention is
$\iota_X\Omega=dH$.

Let $M$ be a smooth manifold. The exterior derivative is an
$\mathbb R$-linear map $d:\Omega^*(M)\to\Omega^*(M)$ of degree one.
For homogeneous smooth forms $\alpha\in\Omega^p(M)$ and
$\beta\in\Omega^q(M)$, $$d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^{\deg\alpha}\alpha\wedge d\beta.$$

Let $(U,x^1,\ldots,x^n)$ be a smooth chart on a smooth manifold and
$\omega$ a smooth $k$-form on $U$, with $k\ge0$. Summing over increasing
$k$-tuples $I$, and writing $dx^I=dx^{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge dx^{i_k}$, if $\omega=\sum_I\omega_I\,dx^I$, then $$d\omega=\sum_I d\omega_I\wedge dx^I.$$

Let $\alpha\in\Omega^k(M)$ and $\beta\in\Omega^\ell(M)$. Their **wedge product**
is the differential form defined pointwise by

$$ (\alpha\wedge\beta)_p:=\alpha_p\wedge\beta_p\in\operatorname{Alt}^{k+\ell}(T_pM). $$

The next proposition verifies that this pointwise field is smooth.
